analogy.p: Think of each factor of a as one Lego brick of the same colour. A power such as a⁵ is a tower of five identical bricks. Multiplying two towers (a³ × a²) simply stacks one on top of the other, so you add the heights: five bricks. Dividing removes the bricks the second tower has from the first, so you subtract the heights. Raising a tower to a power (a³)² means building two copies of the tower of height 3, giving 6 bricks, so you multiply. The analogy breaks down when the bricks are different colours: towers of different bases (2³ and 3²) cannot be merged into one coloured tower, which is why the laws only work for the same base.

bullets: The **base** is the number (or letter) being multiplied; the **index** (plural **indices**) says how many copies of the base are multiplied together.
aⁿ means a × a × … × a with n factors of a, so 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, not 2 × 4 = 8.
Power 2 is called **squared** and power 3 is called **cubed**; higher powers are read “to the power 4”, “to the power 5” and so on.
A power applies only to the symbol immediately before it: 3x² means 3 × x × x, whereas (3x)² means 3x × 3x = 9x².
The index of a letter written without a visible index is **1**: x means x¹.
Indices can be used with numbers and with algebra, for example 4³ = 64 and y⁵ = y × y × y × y × y.
Examiners reward answers that are left as a single simplified power, for example 2⁷ or x⁹, unless the question asks for a value.
core.h: What an index is: base, index and the language of powers
core.p: A **power** (also called an **index** or **exponent**) is a short way of writing repeated multiplication of the same number. In 5³ the **base** is 5 and the **index** is 3, and it means 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. The Edexcel specification expects you to use index notation for integer powers and to apply the **index laws** to numerical and algebraic expressions, so you must be fluent in reading and writing this notation. The most common slip is to treat the index as a multiplier (5³ = 15), so always rebuild the repeated multiplication in your head to check.

bullets: 1 raised to any power is 1, and 0 raised to any positive power is 0, so 1⁷⁰ = 1.
Number tip: to find a square root you do not know, use the roots you do know to bracket it, for example √50 lies between √49 = 7 and √64 = 8, so it is just over 7.
core.h: Powers and roots you must recall
core.p: The specification (number strand) says you should **recall integer squares from 2 × 2 to 15 × 15 and the corresponding square roots, the cubes of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 and the corresponding cube roots**. Instant recall of these saves time on both calculator and non-calculator papers, and it makes factorising, solving, Pythagoras and surd questions far quicker. A root is the **inverse** (reverse) of a power: √ asks “what number multiplied by itself gives this?” and ∛ asks “what number multiplied by itself three times gives this?”.

bullets: Law: **aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ**. Example: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷ = 128, and the base stays 2.
The **base does not change**: 2³ × 2⁴ is not 4⁷. Adding the indices never multiplies the bases.
Algebra: x⁴ × x⁵ = x⁹, and x × x⁶ = x⁷ because x is x¹.
With coefficients, **multiply the numbers and add the indices of each letter separately**: 3x² × 4x⁵ = 12x⁷.
With several letters, treat each letter on its own: 2a³b × 5a²b⁴ = 10a⁵b⁵.
The law also works for negative and fractional indices (covered in the next topic): 5³ × 5⁻² = 5¹ = 5.
The law can be used in reverse: x⁷ = x³ × x⁴, which is useful when expanding or factorising.
Check: write both out in full for small numbers, for example 2² × 2³ = 4 × 8 = 32 = 2⁵.
core.h: The multiplication law: add the indices
core.p: When you **multiply powers of the same base, add the indices**: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. The reason is that you are simply counting factors: a³ × a² = (a × a × a) × (a × a) = a⁵, which has 3 + 2 = 5 factors of a. This is the single most tested index law at GCSE, and it only works when the **bases are the same**. If a question has different bases, you either cannot combine them or you must first rewrite them with a common base (see the section on rewriting bases).

bullets: Law: **aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ**. Example: 5⁸ ÷ 5⁵ = 5³ = 125.
Always **top minus bottom**: x³ ÷ x⁷ = x⁻⁴ = 1/x⁴, not x⁴.
Fraction form: 12x⁷/(4x³) = 3x⁴, because 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 7 − 3 = 4.
Different letters do not combine: 6a⁵b³ ÷ 3a²b = 2a³b², with each letter handled separately.
If the indices are equal the answer is 1: a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰ = 1, which is the reason a⁰ = 1.
Division law can be written with fractions: (aᵐ)/(aⁿ) = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, and the numerical coefficients are simplified as ordinary fractions.
Common error: subtracting the coefficients as well (12 − 4 = 8). Coefficients are divided, indices are subtracted.
core.h: The division law: subtract the indices
core.p: When you **divide powers of the same base, subtract the indices**: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ. The reason is cancelling: a⁵ ÷ a² = (a × a × a × a × a)/(a × a), and two pairs of a cancel, leaving a³. Note that you subtract **bottom from top** (denominator index from numerator index), which can give a zero or negative index, and these are perfectly valid answers. When there are coefficients, divide the numbers (cancelling any common factor) and subtract the indices of each letter separately.

bullets: Law: **(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ**. Example: (5²)³ = 5⁶ = 15 625.
Product in a bracket: **(ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ**. Example: (3xy²)³ = 27x³y⁶.
Quotient in a bracket: (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ. Example: (2/x)³ = 8/x³.
Number and letter indices both change: (2x³)⁴ = 2⁴x³ˣ⁴ = 16x¹².
Do not confuse the two laws: x³ × x² = x⁵ (add) but (x³)² = x⁶ (multiply).
Brackets do not distribute over addition: (a + b)² ≠ a² + b². It equals a² + 2ab + b² (expanding brackets topic).
Combined questions: (2a³)² × 3a = 4a⁶ × 3a = 12a⁷. Work inside-out and tidy at the end.
core.h: The power of a power law and powers of products and quotients
core.p: When a power is raised to another power you **multiply the indices**: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. For example (x³)² = x³ × x³ = x⁶, which has 3 × 2 = 6 factors. When a bracket contains a product, the outside power applies to **every factor inside the bracket, including the number**: (2x³)⁴ = 2⁴ × (x³)⁴ = 16x¹². The same applies to a quotient: (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ. Forgetting to raise the number (writing 2x¹²) is a very common lost mark.

bullets: **a⁰ = 1** for every non-zero a. So 7⁰ = 1, (−3)⁰ = 1 and (x²y)⁰ = 1.
**a¹ = a**: a power of 1 changes nothing, so 9¹ = 9.
Reason for a⁰: a³ ÷ a³ = a³⁻³ = a⁰ and a³ ÷ a³ = 1.
The zero index applies only to what it touches: 3x⁰ = 3 × 1 = 3, whereas (3x)⁰ = 1.
Do not write a⁰ = 0. A zero index never gives zero, it gives 1.
0⁰ is not defined at GCSE, so the rule is stated for non-zero a.
core.p: Any non-zero number raised to the power **zero** equals **1**: a⁰ = 1 (for a ≠ 0). This is not a special rule to memorise blindly; it follows from the division law. a³ ÷ a³ must equal 1 because anything divided by itself is 1, but the division law says a³ ÷ a³ = a³⁻³ = a⁰, so a⁰ = 1. The pattern of powers of 2 shows the same thing: going down one power each time halves the value (8, 4, 2, 1), so the next term after 2¹ = 2 is 2⁰ = 1. A number raised to the power **one** is just the number itself.

bullets: Step 1: apply any power outside a bracket to **every** part inside it (numbers too).
Step 2: multiply or divide the **numerical coefficients**, simplifying fractions as needed.
Step 3: for each letter, use the index law that matches the operation: add (×), subtract (÷), multiply (power of a power).
Step 4: write the answer neatly with the number first, then letters in alphabetical order.
Example: (3x²y)³ ÷ (9xy²) = 27x⁶y³ ÷ 9xy² = 3x⁵y.
Example: 4a²b × 3ab⁵ = 12a³b⁶, because b = b¹ so the indices of b are 1 + 5.
Example: 15p⁷q² ÷ 5p²q = 3p⁵q.
A letter that cancels completely vanishes: 6xy³ ÷ 2xy³ = 3.
core.h: Working with coefficients and several letters
core.p: Most algebraic index questions combine a number part (the **coefficient**) with one or more letters. The safest method is to deal with the pieces **separately**: first the numbers (multiply or divide as normal, and raise to any outside power), then each letter on its own by adding, subtracting or multiplying indices. Write the answer with the number first and the letters in alphabetical order. This organised approach is what earns the method marks in three-mark simplification questions, and you should show an intermediate line so that an arithmetic slip still scores partial credit.

bullets: Common bases to spot: 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 are powers of 2; 9, 27, 81 are powers of 3; 25, 125 are powers of 5; 100, 1000 are powers of 10.
Example: 8² × 4³ = (2³)² × (2²)³ = 2⁶ × 2⁶ = 2¹² = 4096.
Example: 9³ = (3²)³ = 3⁶ = 729.
Example: 2⁸ ÷ 4² = 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁴ = 16.
Different bases cannot be combined by the laws: 2³ × 3² is just 8 × 9 = 72.
Always say what you are doing (“4 = 2²”) so the examiner can award the method mark.
Link: this is exactly the idea used to solve index equations such as 4ˣ = 32.
core.p: The multiplication and division laws need the **same base**. When two numbers look different but are powers of the same small number, rewrite them first. For example 4 = 2² and 8 = 2³, so 4³ × 2⁵ = (2²)³ × 2⁵ = 2⁶ × 2⁵ = 2¹¹. This is the key skill behind “write as a single power of 2” questions and behind solving equations with the unknown in the index. It relies on the power of a power law, so the two laws are often tested together. Knowing the powers of 2, 3 and 5 from the recall list makes this fast.

bullets: Step 1: write each side as a power of the same base (32 = 2⁵).
Step 2: equate the indices, because if aˣ = aʸ with the same base a then x = y.
Step 3: solve the equation you get. Example: 3ˣ⁺¹ = 81 gives 3ˣ⁺¹ = 3⁴, so x + 1 = 4 and x = 3.
Example: 2²ˣ⁻¹ = 32 gives 2x − 1 = 5, so x = 3.
Example: 5ˣ = 1/25 = 5⁻² gives x = −2 (needs negative indices).
Check by substituting back: 3³⁺¹ = 3⁴ = 81 ✓.
If the answer is not a whole number the question may give a calculator route or ask you to leave it as a fraction.
core.h: Solving simple equations with the unknown as an index
core.p: A common Higher-style question gives an equation such as 2ˣ = 32 or 3ˣ⁺¹ = 81 and asks for x. The method is to write both sides as **powers of the same base**, and then, because the powers are equal and the base is the same, the **indices must be equal**. You then solve the resulting ordinary equation. Many such questions are solved by recall of the powers (2⁵ = 32 means x = 5), but showing the base-matching step is what earns the method mark when the equation has an expression in the index.

bullets: √49 = 7 because 7² = 49, but the equation x² = 49 has two solutions: x = ±7.
∛64 = 4 because 4³ = 64; a negative number has a cube root (∛(−8) = −2) but no real square root.
Product and quotient: √(ab) = √a × √b and √(a/b) = √a/√b, so √36 × √4 = √144 = 12.
Roots do not split over addition: √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5, but √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7.
Estimating: √30 lies between √25 = 5 and √36 = 6, and is about 5.5 (actual value 5.477…).
Calculator: use the √ and ∛ keys, and put the whole expression in brackets, for example √(3.5² + 4.2²).
The area of a square with side s is s² and the volume of a cube is s³, so roots reverse these: a square of area 81 cm² has side √81 = 9 cm.
core.p: A **square root** of a number is a value which, multiplied by itself, gives that number; the **cube root** is a value which, multiplied by itself twice (three factors in all), gives that number. The symbols are √ and ∛. Roots are the **inverses** of powers, which is why √(x²) = x for x ≥ 0 and ∛(x³) = x. Every positive number has **two** square roots, one positive and one negative, but the symbol √ gives only the positive one. When solving x² = 49 you must give both answers, x = 7 or x = −7; the Edexcel paper often rewards this explicitly.

bullets: An odd power of a negative number is negative (−2)³ = −8; an even power is positive (−2)⁴ = 16.
2 + 3 × 4² = 2 + 3 × 16 = 2 + 48 = 50: indices first, then ×, then +.
(2 + 3)² = 25 but 2² + 3² = 13, so brackets change the order.
Calculator: for 4.5³ use the cube or power key; for (−5)⁴ type the brackets, otherwise some calculators give −625.
Calculator: use the fraction key for √(a/b) or put the fraction in brackets.
Always write down the unrounded value before rounding, and round only at the end.
core.h: Order of operations, negatives and the calculator
core.p: In **BIDMAS** (or BODMAS) the I stands for **indices** (orders): after brackets, indices are done before multiplication, division, addition and subtraction. This matters with negative numbers: (−3)² = 9 because the bracket means the whole of −3 is squared, but −3² = −9 because only the 3 is squared and then the minus sign is applied. The same care is needed on the calculator: always use brackets around negative bases, and use the power key (xʸ, ^) or the x² and x³ keys correctly. Calculator errors with indices are among the most common ways to lose accuracy marks on Paper 2 and 3.

bullets: Standard form: (2 × 10⁴) × (3 × 10⁵) = 6 × 10⁹ uses the multiplication law for the powers of 10.
Compound growth: £1000 at 5% for 3 years = 1000 × 1.05³; the power counts the number of years.
Similarity: lengths scale by k, areas by k² and volumes by k³.
Algebra: x² × x³ = x⁵ is the same law used when expanding brackets such as x(x² + 3x).
Pitfall: aᵐ + aⁿ cannot be simplified by an index law, since the laws only apply to multiplication, division and powers.
Pitfall: 2³ × 3³ = 6³ (same index, the product of the bases) is valid, but 2³ × 3² has no single-power form.
Higher extension: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, a^(1/2) = √a, a^(1/3) = ∛ a, and a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ.
Exam strategy: write the law you are using in brackets next to the line, which clarifies your method for the examiner.
core.h: Common pitfalls, links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: The index laws underpin many other parts of the specification. **Standard form** uses powers of 10 (3.2 × 10⁴), **compound interest and growth and decay** use a power in the multiplier (1.05ⁿ), **surds** use roots, **area and volume scale factors** use squares and cubes, **quadratics and algebraic fractions** use x² and x³, and **iteration and sequences** use powers. Higher tier extends the laws to **negative and fractional indices**, covered in the next spec point (a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ and a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a). Seeing these links helps you recognise an index question even when it is disguised.

bullets: Step 1: build a factor tree until every branch ends in a **prime**.
Step 2: write the product using indices, for example 144 = 2⁴ × 3².
Step 3: for √, **halve each index**; for ∛, **divide each index by 3**.
If an index does not divide exactly, the root is **not an integer** (for example √72 = √(2³ × 3²) is not whole).
Check by squaring or cubing your answer.
core.h: Finding roots with prime factors (no calculator)
core.p: When a number is not on your recall list you can find its square or cube root by writing it as a product of **prime factors**. Split the number with a factor tree, group the primes into pairs for a square root (or threes for a cube root), and take one from each group. This is a reliable non-calculator method and it connects roots with the index laws, because each group is a power. For example 144 = 2⁴ × 3² = (2² × 3)² so √144 = 2² × 3 = 12, and 216 = 2³ × 3³ = (2 × 3)³ so ∛216 = 6.

bullets: Order of work: **brackets, then indices**, then multiply and divide.
Cross-check one answer by estimating: 2⁸ ÷ 2⁶ should be 256 ÷ 64 = 4.
Keep the answer as a **single power** unless asked for a value.
core.h: Evaluating index expressions without a calculator
core.p: Non-calculator papers reward clear, ordered working with the index laws rather than long multiplication. First simplify using the laws, then evaluate the small power that is left. For example (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁶ = 2⁸ ÷ 2⁶ = 2² = 4, which is far quicker than working out 256 ÷ 64 by hand. Combine the laws with the recall list (squares, cubes, powers of 2, 3, 5 and 10) and write each law in brackets beside the line so the method is visible.

exam: **Command words**: “Simplify” means write as a single, tidy term; “Work out” means give a numerical value; “Write as a single power of 2” means give the answer in the form 2ⁿ.
**1-mark** questions are usually direct recall: “Work out 4³” (64), or “Write down the value of √144” (12). Know your squares and cubes.
**2-mark** simplifications such as “Simplify x⁴ × x⁷” award 1 mark for a correct index (e.g. x¹¹ or x with wrong power but correct method) and 1 for the final answer.
**3-mark** questions with coefficients and brackets, such as (3x²y)³ ÷ 9xy², award marks for 27x⁶y³ (the expansion), then the division of numbers, and then the final answer 3x⁵y.
Always show the intermediate line, for example (2x³)⁴ = 16x¹². Method marks are awarded if the final answer is wrong.
In “write as a power of 2” questions, state the conversions (8 = 2³, 4 = 2²) clearly; the first mark is usually for expressing the bases correctly.
In equations with unknown indices, equate the **indices** once the bases match, then solve; a typical full answer is 3 marks.
When solving x² = k, give **both** roots, ±√k. The wording in the mark scheme is often “x = 7 and x = −7”.
Quote the law in words if asked to “explain”: “When multiplying powers of the same base you add the indices.”
Calculator papers: use brackets around negative bases and check with a rough estimate; non-calculator papers: use the recall facts.
Do not round intermediate answers. Leave answers as exact powers unless told to give a value.
**Non-calculator roots:** use prime factors (144 = 2⁴ × 3²) or the recall list, and show the grouping so the method mark is secured.

mistakes.r: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷; the base stays the same and only the indices are added.
Add the indices: 12x⁷. Multiplying the indices is only for a power of a power.
(x³)² = x⁶; for a power of a power, multiply the indices.
a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a, because a³ ÷ a³ = 1.
(2x³)⁴ = 16x¹²; the outside power applies to every factor in the bracket, including the number.
5³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125; the index counts how many times the base is a factor.
−3² = −9 (only the 3 is squared) but (−3)² = 9 (the bracket is squared).
Divide the coefficients and subtract the indices: 3x⁴.
√(9 + 16) = √25 = 5; roots do not split over addition.
2³ × 3² has no single-power form; evaluate 8 × 9 = 72. The laws need the same base.

summary: Use index notation and the index laws (add for multiplying, subtract for dividing, multiply for a power of a power) with numbers and algebra, including zero and unit indices, and recall squares to 15², cubes of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 and their roots. This underpins standard form, algebra, surds and growth questions across the whole GCSE.

terms.d: The small raised number that shows how many times the base is multiplied by itself, for example the 3 in 5³.
The number or letter that is being multiplied by itself in a power, for example the 5 in 5³.
A number written as a base with an index, such as 2⁴; also a name for the index itself.
Raised to the power 2, so multiplied by itself; the area of a square of side a is a².
Raised to the power 3; the volume of a cube of side a is a³.
A number that, when multiplied by itself, gives the original number; the inverse operation of squaring, written √.
A number that, when used as a factor three times, gives the original number; the inverse of cubing, written ∛.
1 divided by the number; the reciprocal of a is 1/a and corresponds to the index −1.
The number multiplying a letter in an algebraic term, for example 3 in 3x².
The rules for simplifying powers of the same base: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ.
Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1, a⁰ = 1.
Write an expression in its shortest and most efficient form, for example as a single power.
The order of operations: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction.
An operation that reverses another; roots reverse powers.
A whole number, positive, negative or zero.
A factor that is a prime number; every integer greater than 1 is a product of prime factors, for example 144 = 2⁴ × 3².
A power raised to another power, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, found by multiplying the indices.
